hints: Focus on what actually sets the pH here, it is not the oxide itself but how much hydroxide dissolves in a saturated solution.
Remember each oxide forms its hydroxide, $\text{M(OH)}_2$, and solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes in a clear way down the group.
Connect higher solubility to higher $\text{OH}^-$ concentration, then pick the metal lowest down Group 2 for the highest pH.
walkthrough:
**Write what happens in water**

Great start, let us see what is really in solution. Each oxide reacts to make the hydroxide.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{MO(s) + H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_2\text{(aq)}$$

**Recall the solubility trend**

Here is the key Group 2 pattern. Hydroxides become more soluble as you go down the group.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2 < \text{Ca(OH)}_2 < \text{Sr(OH)}_2 < \text{Ba(OH)}_2 \text{ (increasing solubility)}$$

**Link solubility to pH**

A saturated solution holds as much dissolved solid as possible. More soluble means more $\text{OH}^-$ ions released.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{M(OH)}_2\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq) + 2OH}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Pick the highest pH**

Higher $[\text{OH}^-]$ means higher pH. Barium is lowest down this list, so barium hydroxide is most soluble and gives the most alkaline saturated solution.

options.A: Correct. BaO forms $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, which is the most soluble of the four hydroxides. In a saturated solution it gives the highest $[\text{OH}^-]$, so the highest pH.
options.B: Not correct. CaO forms $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, which is more soluble than $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ but much less soluble than $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$. Students sometimes pick calcium because limewater is familiar, but barium gives a higher pH.
options.C: Not correct. MgO forms $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, which is the least soluble hydroxide here and is only sparingly soluble. It gives the lowest $[\text{OH}^-]$ and therefore the lowest pH of the four saturated solutions.
options.D: Not correct. SrO forms $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$, which is quite soluble and gives a high pH, second only to barium. The trap is stopping one step too high up Group 2, solubility still increases from Sr to Ba.
